title: How do you process a very large dataset inside a @Scheduled job without running out of memory, blocking too long, overloading the database, or losing progress on errors?
shortTitle: Processing a large dataset in a @Scheduled job — memory, long execution, DB load, error handling
topicTitle: How do you process a very large dataset inside a @Scheduled job without running

s1_definition.profdef: A scheduled job that loads millions of rows at once risks four problems. MEMORY: `findAll()` into a `List` materialises every row and entity in the heap, causing `OutOfMemoryError`; the fix is to process in CHUNKS/PAGES (keyset pagination or a `Stream`) and flush+clear the persistence context per chunk so entities are garbage-collected. LONG EXECUTION: a single-threaded loop over millions of rows may run for hours and overlap the next scheduled trigger; the fix is to bound the work per run, commit per chunk, and make the job idempotent and resumable. DB LOAD: hammering the database with unbounded queries or huge `IN` clauses starves other traffic; the fix is batched reads/writes, a sensible fetch size, throttling, and running off-peak against a replica where possible. ERRORS: an exception midway can abort the whole job and lose progress; the fix is per-chunk transactions so completed chunks stay committed, recording a cursor/checkpoint, skipping-and-logging poison records, and alerting. In Spring the robust pattern is chunk-oriented processing (Spring Batch) or a hand-written paged loop with per-chunk transactions.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must recalculate interest on ten million accounts every night. Trying to pull all ten million files onto one desk at once collapses the desk (out of memory). The fix is to work through them a tray of five hundred at a time, finishing and filing each tray before fetching the next (chunking), stamping a bookmark after each tray so a crash can resume (checkpoint), not overwhelming the archive clerk with requests (throttling the database), and setting aside any unreadable file to review later instead of abandoning the whole night's work (skip-and-log).
s1_definition.oneliner: For a huge scheduled job, process in chunks with per-chunk transactions and flush+clear the persistence context, bound the work and make it idempotent/resumable via a checkpoint, throttle database load, and skip-and-log bad records instead of aborting — or use Spring Batch's chunk-oriented model.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A scheduled job that loads millions of rows at once risks four problems. MEMORY: `findAll()` into a `List` materialises every row and entity in the heap, causing `OutOfMemoryError`; the fix is to process in CHUNKS/PAGES (keyset pagination or a `Stream`) and flush+clear the persistence context per chunk so entities are garbage-collected. LONG EXECUTION: a single-threaded loop over millions of rows may run for hours and overlap the next scheduled trigger; the fix is to bound the work per run, commit per chunk, and make the job idempotent and resumable. DB LOAD: hammering the database with unbounded queries or huge `IN` clauses starves other traffic; the fix is batched reads/writes, a sensible fetch size, throttling, and running off-peak against a replica where possible. ERRORS: an exception midway can abort the whole job and lose progress; the fix is per-chunk transactions so completed chunks stay committed, recording a cursor/checkpoint, skipping-and-logging poison records, and alerting. In Spring the robust pattern is chunk-oriented processing (Spring Batch) or a hand-written paged loop with per-chunk transactions.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India must recalculate interest on ten million accounts every night. Trying to pull all ten million files onto one desk at once collapses the desk (out of memory). The fix is to work through them a tray of five hundred at a time, finishing and filing each tray before fetching the next (chunking), stamping a bookmark after each tray so a crash can resume (checkpoint), not overwhelming the archive clerk with requests (throttling the database), and setting aside any unreadable file to review later instead of abandoning the whole night's work (skip-and-log).

**One line to remember:** For a huge scheduled job, process in chunks with per-chunk transactions and flush+clear the persistence context, bound the work and make it idempotent/resumable via a checkpoint, throttle database load, and skip-and-log bad records instead of aborting — or use Spring Batch's chunk-oriented model.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the nightly interest-accrual job at National Bank of India that this pattern rescued.

Problem 1 — the job ran out of memory. The first version called `accountRepo.findAll()` to load every savings account and crashed with `OutOfMemoryError` once the bank grew past a few hundred thousand accounts. This is exactly the memory problem: loading all rows and entities at once. The fix is keyset-paged chunks with flush+clear per chunk.

Problem 2 — a failure near the end wasted the whole run. The job ran in one big transaction, and an exception on one corrupt account rolled back millions of already-computed accruals. This is exactly the error problem: per-chunk transactions keep completed chunks committed, and skip-and-log handles the one bad record without aborting.

Problem 3 — the job overloaded the database and slowed morning banking. It read and wrote as fast as possible and saturated the primary database. This is exactly the DB-load problem: bounded chunk sizes, batched writes, and a small throttle pause keep the job from starving live traffic.

Problem 4 — restarts started from scratch. When the job was restarted after a crash, it reprocessed everything. This is exactly the long-execution/resumability problem: a checkpoint cursor lets the job resume from the last committed chunk, and idempotent updates make re-running a chunk safe.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is an `Account` entity. The `InterestAccrualJob` has a `@Scheduled` method that delegates to the service. The `InterestAccrualService` processes accounts in KEYSET-PAGED chunks of five hundred, each chunk in its own `@Transactional` method that recalculates interest, flushes and clears the persistence context, records a checkpoint cursor, throttles briefly between chunks, and skips-and-logs any poison record. A `JobCheckpoint` entity stores the last processed cursor so a restart resumes. A test verifies the chunking advances the cursor and that a poison record is skipped rather than aborting the chunk. The code notes Spring Batch as the production-grade alternative.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the nightly interest-accrual run over all savings accounts.

Step 1 — entry and checkpoint. At 01:00 the `@Scheduled` method fires and delegates to `service.run()`. The service reads the checkpoint cursor for the job; on a fresh run it is empty, and on a restart after a crash it holds the last committed account id, so processing resumes from there rather than from the start.

Step 2 — bounded chunk read. The service reads the next chunk with keyset pagination: `SELECT a FROM Account a WHERE a.accountId > :cursor ORDER BY a.accountId` limited to five hundred rows. This bounds both memory (only five hundred entities in the heap) and database load (a small indexed read), and because it is keyset rather than offset, deep chunks stay fast.

Step 3 — per-chunk transaction and processing. `processChunk` runs in its own `@Transactional` method. For each account it computes the idempotent daily accrual (setting, not adding, today's value, so re-running the chunk after a restart produces the same result). If one account throws, the service skips-and-logs it and continues rather than aborting the chunk.

Step 4 — flush, clear, commit. After processing the chunk, the service calls `flush` to write the updates and `clear` to detach the five hundred entities so they can be garbage-collected, preventing the persistence context from growing unbounded. The chunk transaction commits, so this chunk's work is now durable regardless of what happens later.

Step 5 — checkpoint and throttle. The service advances the checkpoint cursor to the last account id in the chunk and commits that too, so a crash now resumes from this point. It then sleeps briefly to avoid saturating the database, and loops to the next chunk. When a read returns fewer than five hundred rows the set is exhausted; the service resets the cursor for next night and logs the totals, including how many poison records were skipped.

```
2026-10-24 01:03:10 INFO  InterestAccrualJob - Starting nightly interest accrual job
2026-10-24 01:03:10 FINE  InterestAccrualService - chunk read WHERE account_id > '' LIMIT 500 → 500 rows
2026-10-24 01:03:10 FINE  InterestAccrualService - processChunk committed; flush+clear released 500 entities
2026-10-24 01:03:10 WARNING InterestAccrualService - Skipping account SAV0777: null interest_rate (poison, logged)
2026-10-24 01:03:10 FINE  InterestAccrualService - checkpoint cursor=SAV0500 (resumable); throttle 50ms
2026-10-24 01:08:42 INFO  InterestAccrualJob - Nightly accrual finished: processed=10000000, skipped=3, chunks=20000
```

```
  @Scheduled(cron 01:00) → InterestAccrualJob.nightlyAccrual()
    │
    ▼
  InterestAccrualService.run()
    │ read checkpoint cursor (resume point)
    ▼
  ┌─ LOOP per chunk ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ read: WHERE account_id > :cursor ORDER BY account_id LIMIT 500 (keyset, bounded)
  │   │
  │   ▼
  │ processChunk(...) @Transactional   ← PER-CHUNK commit
  │   for each account: accrueDaily (idempotent)
  │     on error → SKIP-AND-LOG (poison record), continue
  │   flush() → write chunk
  │   clear() → detach 500 entities → GC (prevents OutOfMemoryError)
  │   COMMIT chunk (durable)
  │   │
  │   ▼
  │ advance checkpoint cursor = last account_id (resumable)
  │ throttle 50ms (good DB citizen)
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    │ read < 500 → done
    ▼
  totals: processed / skipped / chunks

  ── FOUR RISKS → FIXES ──
  memory       : findAll() → chunked paging + flush+clear per chunk
  long run     : bound work + per-chunk commit + resumable checkpoint
  DB load      : bounded reads + batched writes + throttle + off-peak/replica
  errors       : per-chunk txn + skip-and-log poison + checkpoint + alerts
  (production : Spring Batch = chunk model + JobRepository + restart + skip/retry)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Processing a very large dataset in a scheduled job has four risks, and I address each deliberately. The first is memory: loading everything with findAll into a list materialises every row and entity in the heap and causes an out-of-memory error, so I process in bounded chunks using keyset pagination or a stream, and after each chunk I flush and clear the persistence context so the processed entities detach and get garbage-collected. The second is long execution: a single run over millions of rows can last hours and overlap the next trigger, so I bound the work, commit per chunk so progress is durable, and prevent overlapping runs. The third is database load: unbounded queries and tight loops starve live traffic, so I use bounded chunk reads, batched writes, a small throttle between chunks, and I run off-peak or against a replica. The fourth, and most important for correctness, is error handling: if the job runs as one giant transaction and fails near the end, everything rolls back, so I use per-chunk transactions, record a checkpoint cursor so a restart resumes where it stopped, make the updates idempotent so re-running a chunk is safe, and skip-and-log individual poison records instead of aborting.

In our nightly interest-accrual job at National Bank of India, the first version called findAll and crashed with out-of-memory once we grew past a few hundred thousand accounts, and a failure near the end once rolled back millions of computed accruals. We rebuilt it to process five hundred accounts per keyset-paged chunk, each chunk in its own transaction with a flush and clear afterwards, advancing a checkpoint cursor so a crash resumes from the last committed chunk, throttling briefly between chunks so morning banking is not slowed, and skipping-and-logging the occasional corrupt account rather than failing the whole run. The daily accrual is idempotent because it sets rather than adds today's value, so re-running a chunk never double-counts.

The senior recommendation I always add is that for genuinely large, restartable, auditable batch work the production-grade answer is Spring Batch, which gives chunk-oriented processing, a job repository that persists progress, restartability, skip and retry policies, and metrics out of the box. A hand-written paged loop with per-chunk transactions is fine for moderate volumes, but Spring Batch is what I reach for when the dataset is huge and the job must be resumable and observable.
